title: What is `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` — a command to sync partition metadata between the file system (HDFS/S3) and the metastore when partitions are added or removed outside of Spark SQL?

s1_definition.profdef: `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` is a Spark SQL and Hive command that scans the storage location of a partitioned external table, discovers partition directories that physically exist on disk (HDFS or S3) but are not yet recorded in the metastore, and adds those partition entries to the catalog. It reconciles the gap that appears when files are written to partition folders by tools other than the SQL engine, because the metastore only knows about partitions it was explicitly told about.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps a master index card box (the metastore) that lists every daily folder of trade records, like `date=2026-10-28`, `date=2026-10-29`. A separate batch job from the risk team drops a brand new folder `date=2026-10-30` straight into the storage room (S3) without updating the index card box. When Rajesh runs a query for the 30th, the catalog says "I have no card for that date" and returns nothing, even though the data is physically sitting there. `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` is the clerk who walks the storage room, sees the new folder, and writes a fresh index card for it so queries find the data.
s1_definition.oneliner: `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` makes the metastore catch up with partition folders that already exist on disk but were added outside the SQL engine.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` is a Spark SQL and Hive command that scans the storage location of a partitioned external table, discovers partition directories that physically exist on disk (HDFS or S3) but are not yet recorded in the metastore, and adds those partition entries to the catalog. It reconciles the gap that appears when files are written to partition folders by tools other than the SQL engine, because the metastore only knows about partitions it was explicitly told about.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India keeps a master index card box (the metastore) that lists every daily folder of trade records, like `date=2026-10-28`, `date=2026-10-29`. A separate batch job from the risk team drops a brand new folder `date=2026-10-30` straight into the storage room (S3) without updating the index card box. When Rajesh runs a query for the 30th, the catalog says "I have no card for that date" and returns nothing, even though the data is physically sitting there. `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` is the clerk who walks the storage room, sees the new folder, and writes a fresh index card for it so queries find the data.

**One line to remember:** `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` makes the metastore catch up with partition folders that already exist on disk but were added outside the SQL engine.

sections.s2_technical:
A partitioned table in Spark or Hive stores data in a directory layout where each partition value becomes a folder, such as `.../trades/trade_date=2026-10-30/part-0000.parquet`. The metastore holds a list of these partitions so the query planner can prune directories. When you write data using Spark SQL with `INSERT INTO ... PARTITION`, the metastore is updated automatically. The problem is when an external process, like a streaming job, a `aws s3 cp` upload, or another team's pipeline, drops files into new partition folders directly. The metastore has no idea those folders exist, so queries silently skip them.

`MSCK REPAIR TABLE trades` fixes this. It lists the table's base path, finds every folder that matches the partition column pattern, compares that set against the partitions registered in the metastore, and adds the missing ones. For example `spark.sql("MSCK REPAIR TABLE trades")` discovers `trade_date=2026-10-30` and registers it.

A senior-level nuance is that plain `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` only adds partitions; it does not remove partitions whose folders were deleted. For that you use `MSCK REPAIR TABLE trades SYNC PARTITIONS` (or the ADD/DROP variants) which both adds new and drops stale partitions. A finer-grained alternative when you know exactly what changed is `ALTER TABLE trades ADD PARTITION (trade_date='2026-10-30') LOCATION '...'`, which is far cheaper than a full repair because `MSCK` has to list the entire directory tree, and on S3 with millions of partitions that listing is slow and expensive. In production on object stores, many teams avoid `MSCK` entirely and instead call `ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION` from the writing job, or move to Delta Lake which tracks files in a transaction log and needs no repair at all. The command only applies to external/unmanaged partitioned tables where Spark controls metadata but not necessarily the writes.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, settled trades are written to a data lake folder partitioned by trade date. A nightly settlement job owned by the operations team writes directly to S3-style storage (here we simulate with the local file system), creating a new `trade_date=...` folder each night. The analytics table over this location is an external partitioned table. The next morning Priya from the analytics team runs a query for yesterday's trades and gets zero rows, even though she can see the folder exists. This is exactly the metastore-out-of-sync problem: the folder exists on disk but the catalog has no partition entry, so the planner prunes it away.

This is exactly how `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` works. The command scans the table location, finds the new `trade_date` folder that the operations job created, and registers it as a partition so the analytics query finally returns the rows.

Problem 2 — Later the compliance team purges a very old partition folder to meet a data-retention rule, deleting `trade_date=2020-01-01` directly from storage. Now the metastore still lists a partition whose folder is gone, and queries touching it fail or return errors. The plain repair does not help here because it only adds. We need the SYNC behavior that also drops stale partitions.

In the mini-project we build a small runnable demo that simulates this partitioned-lake lifecycle without a real metastore, using an in-memory catalog so the logic is clear. We create a `PartitionedTradeLake` that owns a base directory and an in-memory partition catalog. A `ExternalWriter` writes trade files into new date folders directly, bypassing the catalog, to mimic an outside job. A `MetastoreRepairService` implements the `repair()` logic: list folders on disk, compare with the catalog, add missing partitions, and in sync mode drop partitions whose folders vanished. A `TradeQueryService` answers a query for a given date but only sees data if the partition is registered, proving why repair matters. The demo steps: write two partitions through the catalog normally, write one partition externally so it is invisible, show the query returns nothing, run repair, show the query now works, delete a folder, run sync repair, and show the stale partition is removed.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
lake:
  base-path: /tmp/nbi-trade-lake/trades
  partition-column: trade_date
  repair:
    sync-partitions: true   # when true, repair also drops stale partitions
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three trade-date folders on disk (`2026-10-28`, `2026-10-29`, `2026-10-30`) and a catalog that initially knows only the first two.

Step 1: The writer creates the folder `trade_date=2026-10-28` and writes one trade row, and the code immediately registers the partition. The data on disk and the catalog entry both exist, so they agree. The same happens for `2026-10-29`.

Step 2: An external job creates `trade_date=2026-10-30` with two trade rows but never touches the catalog. Now the disk has three folders while the catalog has only two. The data is physically present but invisible to the planner.

Step 3: Priya queries the 30th. The query service checks `isRegistered("2026-10-30")`, finds it is not in the catalog, and returns zero without even looking at the file. This is the silent-missing-data symptom.

Step 4: The repair service lists the disk folders and gets the set of three dates, compares against the catalog set of two, finds `2026-10-30` is the difference, and registers it. The catalog now has all three.

Step 5: Priya queries the 30th again. This time the partition is registered, the service reads the file, counts two rows, and returns 2.

Step 6: Compliance deletes the `2026-10-28` folder from storage. The catalog still lists it, so now the catalog is ahead of the disk — a stale partition.

Step 7: A sync repair lists the disk (now two folders), compares with the catalog (three partitions), finds `2026-10-28` has no folder, and unregisters it. The catalog ends with exactly the two partitions that physically exist.

Final output:

```
Oct 30, 2026 7:02:11 AM com.bank.lake.ExternalWriter writeExternally
WARNING: External job wrote folder /tmp/nbi-trade-lake/trades/trade_date=2026-10-30 WITHOUT updating the catalog (metastore now out of sync)
Oct 30, 2026 7:02:11 AM com.bank.lake.TradeQueryService countTradesForDate
WARNING: Query for 2026-10-30 returns 0 rows: partition NOT in catalog (even if data exists on disk)
INFO: Before repair, 2026-10-30 count = 0
Oct 30, 2026 7:02:11 AM com.bank.lake.MetastoreRepairService repair
INFO: REPAIR added missing partition: 2026-10-30
INFO: After repair, 2026-10-30 count = 2
WARNING: REPAIR dropped stale partition: 2026-10-28
INFO: Final catalog partitions: [2026-10-29, 2026-10-30]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  External settlement job
    │ writes files directly to storage
    ▼
  S3/HDFS: trades/trade_date=2026-10-30/part-0000.csv   ← data EXISTS
    │
    │   (catalog NOT updated)
    ▼
  Metastore catalog: knows {2026-10-28, 2026-10-29}      ← data INVISIBLE
    │
    ▼
  Query: count where trade_date=2026-10-30
    │ planner prunes → partition not registered
    ▼
  Result: 0 rows  ✗  (wrong — data is on disk)

        │
        │  MSCK REPAIR TABLE trades
        ▼
  Repair: list disk {28,29,30}  vs  catalog {28,29}
    │ diff = {30} → ADD
    ▼
  Metastore catalog: now {28, 29, 30}
    │
    ▼
  Query: count where trade_date=2026-10-30 → 2 rows ✓

  ── SYNC branch (folder deleted) ──
  compliance deletes trade_date=2026-10-28 folder
    │ MSCK REPAIR TABLE trades SYNC PARTITIONS
    ▼
  Repair: list disk {29,30} vs catalog {28,29,30}
    │ stale = {28} → DROP
    ▼
  Metastore catalog: {29, 30}  ✓ fully in sync
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
`MSCK REPAIR TABLE` is a Hive and Spark SQL command that reconciles the partition metadata in the metastore with the partition folders that actually exist in the table's storage location. When you have a partitioned external table and files are written into new partition directories by something other than the SQL engine, such as a streaming job, a direct object-store upload, or another team's pipeline, the metastore never learns about those folders and queries silently return no rows for them. Running the repair makes the engine scan the base path, discover the partition folders on disk, and add the missing ones to the catalog so queries can finally see the data.

The important nuance is that the plain command only adds partitions, it does not remove them, so if a folder gets deleted outside the engine you end up with a stale partition that still appears in the catalog. To handle both directions you use the sync partitions variant, which adds new folders and drops partitions whose folders are gone. I also keep in mind that repair is expensive on object stores like S3 because it has to list the entire directory tree, and with millions of partitions that is slow and costly, so the cheaper production pattern is to have the writing job call alter table add partition for exactly the partition it created.

At the National Bank of India I ran into this when the operations settlement batch wrote each night's trades straight to the lake partitioned by trade date, and the analytics team kept getting zero rows for the latest day. The fix was to run the repair so the metastore picked up the new date folder, and I scheduled it right after the settlement job finished. Over time, because the partition count grew large and the repair listing got slow, I moved the writers to register their own partitions explicitly and eventually to Delta Lake, which tracks files in a transaction log and needs no repair at all. That progression is what I would explain in an interview: repair solves the immediate sync gap, but at scale you design the write path so the catalog never drifts in the first place.
